# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What made the others more pressing?

whys.g1: Lena's and Aisha's answers are both about the money being safe and insured, and 'Money must be there and insured' is how I'd name that. My answer is about getting cash back fast to pay bills, and Rachel's is about runway, so neither belongs in that group and leaving them on their own is right.
whys.g2: No answer on this line is junk or off-topic; Rachel's tax-break aside is odd but still about where the cash sits, and it is not grouped anyway.

founder.order_why: It moves from naming and market to the context, then the problem and its checks, then who asks and who gets the link, which is how I'd explain Palus to a stranger: who holds raise cash, how often it earns too little, and what they use today.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 open with the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so the context feels asked twice around the window question. Screens 12 and 15 show the Importance and Current solution checks again after I had already checked them on 11 and 14.
founder.missing: How big the long-term reserve is (for example under $1M, $1M to $5M, over $5M). The yield given up scales with the balance, and a lean startup without much idle cash is not my customer. Nothing asks for the reserve size or uses it to screen people in.

PRIMARY.order_why: It moves sensibly from whether I bank with Mercury-style banks, to whether my raise cash under-earned, to what I'd want easier, to why, and then to how my last placement went.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing asked what it would take for me to move the cash, like the operational burden of switching versus a higher yield, or what rate I'm actually earning now (about 3.2%).

screens.why4: 'Getting cash back fast when needed' and 'Moving money between accounts without mistakes' both describe the monthly transfer from reserve to operating account, so a stranger could see them as one chore.
screens.why5: My problem, earning more on the raise without risking it, leads the list, and the four rivals are the ones I named, kept nearly word for word.
screens.why7: The own row is first and is an -ing act on my verb, there are four rivals, and the belief can be both supported and refuted; but the two liquidity rows overlap, and 'Knowing the months of runway left' leans toward burn forecasting rather than the moment of deciding where cash sits, which bends the rule that no two rows overlap and each stays in the moment.
screens.instead: Your problem and the difficulties you named: Getting the raise to earn more until it's spent · Keeping cash safe above the insured limit · Getting cash back fast when needed · Topping up the operating account each month without mistakes · Sizing how much cash to keep on hand

screens.why1: After naming the other difficulties, it is the obvious point to check the list Keel will read to finance leads and the belief it will test.
screens.why2: The rows are in a finance lead's words, but 'raise cash' is not a phrase we use (we say 'the reserve' or 'cash from the raise'), and the stray 'yours' tag and 'yours + 4' note need a second look.
screens.why3: Yield, runway, safety above the FDIC limit, getting cash back and tracking balances across accounts are all things a finance lead handles each month.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and in my words, but 'Knowing the months of runway left' partly overlaps the own row, because extra yield is pitched exactly as extra runway.
screens.why5: My problem and the rivals I drew from the thread (runway, insured limit, 1-2 day access, reconciliation across accounts) are kept, and nothing names Palus.
screens.why7: The own row is first, on its verb, with four rivals and a belief that can hold or fail, but the runway row is partly a consequence of the own row, which bends the rule that no row is a cause or part of another.
screens.instead: Getting the reserve to earn more · Keeping cash safe above the insured limit · Getting cash back fast when needed · Reconciling cash across several accounts · Deciding how much cash to keep at the bank

screens.why1: Once I've said cash earns less than it could, the obvious next question is what finance leads do with it today and how well that goes; it is the last problem step before the Check.
screens.why2: "Until the company sends it today" stumbles: "sends" should be "spends", and the trailing "today" makes me read it twice; the hint's "checking for errors by hand" is from someone else's trade, not treasury.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my batchmates' reserves sit: the bank's treasury sweep into a money market fund at about 3.5% after fees, and I lived it myself.
screens.why4: Two boxes, one for the act and its means and one for how it goes, plus "I'm not sure" as the founder's escape, is all this screen needs.
screens.why5: My job is money kept safe and earning until the company spends it; "sends it" turns that into a transfer, a small drift from what I typed.
screens.why7: My first box names the act and its means (bank treasury, money market fund, 3.5% after fees), and my four rungs sit on one measure, yield after fees, best to worst, with a working first rung ("Earned a market rate after fees"), so Keel has one worse rung to add and a line under the first by default.
screens.instead: How do finance leads keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it? (first box: where the long-term reserve sits today and with what; second box: how well it earned after fees, best to worst)

screens.why1: Right after I said how my people park the raise today, asking me to check how well that actually earns is the obvious next step before Keel tests whether it falls short.
screens.why2: 'Market rate', 'after fees' and 'sat in checking' are how a startup finance lead talks about treasury yield, and I read every rung on first pass.
screens.why3: A finance lead sees the rate on the Mercury or Brex treasury statement each month, so they know where their last cash review landed.
screens.why4: The first four rungs step down cleanly, but 'The cash sat in checking earning nothing' overlaps 'Earned next to nothing after fees' and describes a different place for the money, not the treasury product doing worse.
screens.why5: The scale is my measure, yield after fees, and the belief about the bank's bundled treasury product is my own pitch: the problem is the treasury product, not the bank.
screens.why7: The measure, the five rungs, the working first rung and the line under it are all met, but the last rung swaps in another place ('sat in checking') instead of the treasury product failing outright on yield, which is the exact off-measure pattern the card names.
screens.instead: Earned a market rate after fees · ┄ line ┄ · Earned a bit under market after fees · Earned well under market after fees · Earned next to nothing after fees · Lost money after fees

screens.why1: Right after my Save on the Current solution Check, this is the reviewed list I would expect: Keel shows me what changed before I move on to the idea.
screens.why2: Earned a market rate, a bit under market, well under market and after fees are how I and any finance lead talk about yield on the reserve, so I can read the five on first pass.
screens.why3: Any finance lead holding raise cash knows roughly what the reserve netted after the treasury product's fee last quarter.
screens.why4: The scale is clean and distinct, but 'market rate' is slippery: a lead earning about 3.5% in Mercury or Brex Treasury will call that market and pick rung 1, though that is the gap I sell against, and the bare 'it' in 'Fees cost more than it earned' reads loosely.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed: yield after fees, graded down, with the bank's bundled treasury product as today's way, which matches 'the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank'.
screens.why7: Every rung is on one measure (yield after fees), there are exactly five in order from best to worst, rung 1 is today's way working with the line under it, and the last is outright failure on that measure (net loss), so the belief can be both supported and refuted.
screens.instead: Rows: Earned what a money market fund pays, after fees · Earned a bit under that after fees · Earned well under that after fees · Earned next to nothing after fees · Fees took more than the reserve earned

screens.why1: Picking who asks my finance leads the questions is the natural last step before the study goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to a founder: a voice to pick, hear it in 5 seconds, 400 credits either way, sent by text message.
screens.why3: I know how finance leads expect to be spoken to, so I can judge from a 5-second sample which voice they would take seriously.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices, each with a sample, a preselected default and the same cost; the screen says people can read and type instead, so no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The screen keeps 'finance leads' as I typed it and shows nothing of Palus's product to the people who will answer.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, deciding how finance leads will answer is the natural next step before sending.
screens.why2: The three options are plain and each says in one line what the finance lead will actually do on the link.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads are busy and would rather read and tap than sit on a video call, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices, and 'Let them choose' is a sensible middle option rather than a redundant one.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my idea or leaks my product to respondents; it only uses my actor word 'finance leads'.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions and how they answer, deciding who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending, and I know my batchmates and finance leads by name.
screens.why2: Plain as typed: people I know by name, a list from a search, or one open link posted in a group like the YC batch Slack -- all words I use.
screens.why3: It asks about my own outreach, which I know exactly: the batchmates who told us they wanted this and the finance leads I can message directly.
screens.why4: The three routes cover how I would reach finance leads (direct, searched list, a post in a founder or finance community), they are distinct, and my pick is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is reworded here; the screen only routes the links, and my answer 'people I know by name' is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is stated, but the number beside it, 'median 2 months out of 3', sits inside my own 2-to-3 band, so it reads like agreement and does not show why the stage is split; the Importance card, 2 short of the bar, is the weaker result and is not in the headline.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence and Current solution read at once (7 of 7, bar 5 of 7), but the Frequency line stacks a median, two counts, the bar and '1 short' into one string I had to read twice.
screens.why_b3: The four dimension names and the statement under the title are my own claims: the 18-to-24-month raise, money untouched for six months, the 3.5% fund with a 0.15% to 0.60% fee, and nobody having time; the belief lines follow my circumstance and job.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what the split on Frequency and Importance means for Palus or what to do about it; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card, but nothing says 7 is a small sample, and 'above your band' sets 7 of 7 against a population claim of 6 to 7 in 10 without that caution.
screens.instead: Problem is split among only 7 finance leads: all 7 say their cash earns less and that the bank's treasury falls short, but only 3 of 7 rank yield in their top two worries (2 short of the bar), and 4 of 7 hit it most months. Find out what they rank above yield before building on yield alone.

screens.why_b1: The status "Holding up above your band" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with my marker at 5, labelled "5 of 7 (at least 6 in 10)", so what is counted, over how many and where my bar sits read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is named Prevalence and keeps my 6 to 7 in 10 band, but "had raise cash earn less than it could" is an awkward rewording of yield given up on the long-term reserve; I recognise it, but it isn't how I'd say it.
screens.why_b4: "Common among these 7" and the pointer to the next two cards tell me where to look, but the card doesn't say what a unanimous Yes means for Palus, such as that even leads content at the bank (Dana, Aisha) say yes, so this alone isn't demand.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and "Common among these 7" claims nothing beyond the seven who answered.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 said their raise cash earned less than it could, above your 6-to-7 band, but only 7 answered and even those happy at their bank said yes, so read Frequency and Importance before treating this as demand.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the number that decides it: 4 of 7 at or beyond my 2 months, against a bar of 5 of 7, so 1 short.
screens.why_b2: The strip plainly shows 7 people, 4 for and 3 against, with the marker at 5, but the chart's tick row starts at 0, which no one could pick, and the legend's 'what you said · at what you said' takes a second look to tell apart.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name is mine and '2 to 3 months out of 3' is my range, but 'Finance leads have raise cash earn less than it could' is garbled and not how I or my trade would say it, and the Asked line tacks 'the most recent time it happened' onto a count question.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me onward without saying what a split on how often the reserve underearns means for the pitch, for example that for 3 of 7 this is a now-and-then review rather than a monthly pain.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible, calls 7 people 'a lean, not a call', and does not dress 4 of 7 up as support, so nothing claims beyond the data.
screens.instead: Frequency: finance leads saw their raise cash earn below market on 2 to 3 of the last 3 months -- 4 of 7 did (bar 5), median 2; a lean split among 7, so for nearly half this is an occasional cash review, not a monthly cost.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right beside '3 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short', so I know it missed and by how much, though for a 3-4 miss I'd rather it plainly said it did not hold.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts picks (14) while the bar is in people (5 of 7) and only appears on the strip below, so it takes a second look to see that my 3 is people and where 5 would land.
screens.why_b3: The belief line and 'Getting raise cash to earn more' are my own row from the launch: earning more on the raise without switching banks, with five rows as I listed them.
screens.why_b4: The So line says I'm 2 short and in a four-way tie with runway, safety above the insured limit and getting cash back fast, but it never says what that means for me, for example that yield isn't the standout hurt and the pitch should lead with safety and liquidity.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and 'a lean, not a call' are said, but 'the 4 who ranked others first' and 'put two others first' read as if yield came second for them, when they left it out of their two entirely.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 3 of 7 put earning more in their two (bar 5), tied with runway, safety and fast access, and the 4 against left it out entirely, so yield alone isn't the hurt; lead with safe and liquid, with yield on top, and test that.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Each rung shows its count, my line sits under "Earned a market rate after fees" with 0 above it, and the strip shows 7 cells all for me with the marker at 5, so I can read what is counted, over how many and where the bar is at once.
screens.why_b3: Current solution is my dimension and the belief keeps my act, keeping raise money in the bank's treasury product, with my after-fees rungs word for word; only "finance leads" is a shortened form of my actor.
screens.why_b4: "Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study" points forward but says nothing about the size of the gap: the biggest group, 3 of 7, earned only a bit under market, and that margin is what my 0.25% fee and my bond risk have to beat.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" is said, and nothing claims more than these seven people.
screens.instead: Say that 3 of 7 were only a bit under market and 4 were well under or worse, so my pitch should lead with the people well under market, and the next study should check whether a small yield gain beats the hassle for the rest.

screens.why_b1: The status word People disagree sits beside 3 of 7 put it in their two, bar 5 of 7, 2 short, so I know the line failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the belief reads Getting raise cash to earn more where I checked earning more without switching banks, so it is reworded but recognisable.
screens.why_b4: The heading When a line fails and the quotes point at safety, insurance and fast access, but nothing says what to change, such as leading with custody, liquidity and insurance before yield.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and the 4 against are visible, and nothing is claimed beyond the four who were asked.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that boards after the bank failures only ask whether the money is insured, that treasury pays monthly bills, or that the accountant wants plain cash for the tax break, and these change my pitch.
screens.instead: Importance failed (3 of 7, bar 5): the four against ranked safety above the insured limit and fast access over yield, so lead with custody and next-day liquidity before the rate.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it obviously checks I'm in the right kind of company before asking about where our raise sits, and nothing has been asked before it.
screens.why2: Mercury and Brex are plain to me, but 'a similar startup bank' made me pause: Brex isn't strictly a bank, and I'd wonder whether SVB, or a big bank with a startup desk, counts.
screens.why3: I run our accounts, so I know exactly where we bank without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No is complete and distinct for a gate, and the guidelines give a gate no escape.
screens.why5: It matches the segment as I'd recognise it, and nothing about the product or a pitch reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question, about 19 words, with two options a listener holds easily.
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its operating cash with Mercury, Brex or another bank built for startups? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury or similar, asking whether our raise money underperformed in the last 3 months is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Did you have raise cash earn less than it could" is broken English, and "raise cash" isn't how I talk; I'd say "the money from our raise", so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know what our cash earned (about 3.2%), but "less than it could" leaves me guessing against what: a higher-yield account I chose not to chase, or money that sat idle in checking?
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the recall chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this gate.
screens.why5: The founder's shorthand "raise cash" comes through nearly raw, and the act has drifted into a judgement about potential yield.
screens.why6: It is short and ends "Yes or no", but "did you have raise cash earn less" stumbles when said aloud and makes you replay it.
screens.why7: Yes and No are the right fixed pair with no escape, but "earn less than it could" is a judgement on a standing state rather than one act in the window, so nearly anyone not in T-bills says Yes and No has thin ground.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did money from your raise sit in an account earning little or nothing? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes at the gate, asking how often follows naturally.
screens.why2: 'Did you have raise cash earn less than it could' is garbled, and I don't call it 'raise cash'; it's our operating cash or the money from the round, so I'd have to read it twice and still guess what's meant.
screens.why3: Our cash sat at about 3.2% every month on purpose, so whether it 'earned less than it could' is a judgement about yields I don't track month by month, and I'd just guess 3.
screens.why4: 1, 2, 3 covers every month in the window without overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: 'Raise cash' and 'earn less than it could' read like someone's pitch about idle cash rather than how I'd put it, so the founder's framing shows through a little.
screens.why6: Short and one question with a clean 1 to 3 list, but 'have raise cash earn less than it could' trips when heard.
screens.why7: The measure, the shape (1 to 3, unit said once) and the escape are all right, but the event is a lasting state (cash earning less) rather than an act that happened in a given month, so a count of months can't be told apart from 'all the time'.
screens.instead: On how many of the last 3 months did you check whether your startup's idle cash could earn more elsewhere? 1 · 2 · 3 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After two screens about our raise cash earning less than it could, asking which part of handling that cash I'd most want made easier is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Raise cash" is not something I'd ever say (it's "the money from the round" or just "our cash"), and "the last 3 months after a raise" reads oddly when we didn't raise in the last 3 months, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: These are all things I actually deal with: sweep and treasury yield, FDIC limits, how fast I can pull money back, and juggling accounts at Mercury and elsewhere.
screens.why4: The rows are mostly distinct and real, but "Knowing the months of runway left" is a forecasting job, not about where the cash sits, and the thing I care about most (not adding operational hassle to manage it) only half shows up as "tracking across several accounts".
screens.why5: No product or company name reaches me, and the yield row still says what the earlier screens asked about.
screens.why6: One short question with five short options read as a list and one escape at the end, easy to hold on a single hearing.
screens.why7: The own row (getting the cash to earn more) is on the list, not first, with four rivals and "None of these" at the first ask, but the runway row sits outside the moment of deciding where the cash is parked, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of where your company's cash from the last round has sat these past few months. Which one would you most like made easier? Getting more yield on idle cash · Keeping cash safe above the FDIC limit · Pulling cash back fast when needed · Managing cash across several accounts · Keeping the setup simple to run · None of these

screens.why1: Asking why I passed over yield right after I ranked what I'd want made easier is the obvious next question, though it names two picks when the screen before asked for one.
screens.why2: It reads back the long rows instead of my words: 'raise cash' is not how I talk, and 'getting cash back fast' could mean card cashback rather than pulling money out of a sweep or T-bill account when we need it.
screens.why3: Yes, I can answer it straight away: the work of moving and reconciling money across accounts matters more to me than a few basis points on top of the roughly 3.2% we already earn.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: 'Raise cash' as a noun reads like someone else's label for our money, so the founder's terms show through a little.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is a 25-word sentence holding two long rows and a comparison before the 'why', so I would have to hold a lot before I get to the question.
screens.instead: You'd rather get money out quickly and keep track of it across accounts than earn more on it. Why is that?

screens.why1: It's the natural last question about how today's setup works, but I had just told you yield matters less to me than getting cash back fast and tracking it, and this asks only about yield.
screens.why2: Treasury product and after fees are my words, but I don't make 'placements' (the cash just sits in Mercury Treasury), and 'market rate' makes me stop and ask which market: T-bills, money funds or high-yield savings.
screens.why3: I know we earn about 3.2% after the fee, but sorting that into 'a bit under' or 'well under market' means guessing a benchmark, and it assumes we use the bank's own treasury product rather than a broker or a money fund.
screens.why4: The rungs are distinct and on one scale, but 'a bit under' and 'well under' have no edge between them, 'fees cost more than it earned' is close to impossible on a sweep product, and anyone holding T-bills elsewhere or leaving cash in checking has no true answer.
screens.why5: Nothing about the founder's product reaches me, and the question stays on raise cash earning less than it could.
screens.why6: One short question and five short parallel options, said as a list I can hold, then one escape.
screens.why7: All five rungs grade yield after fees, run best to worst, start on a working rung and end on a failure, and the escape is there, but the stem names one means (the bank's treasury product) as the act instead of keeping raise cash earning, so other ways of doing the job are left out.
screens.instead: Think of the last 3 months. How did keeping your raise cash earning go? Earned a market rate after fees; earned a bit under market; earned well under market; earned next to nothing; fees cost more than it earned. Or: someone else did it.
